text: Your own code is usually the smallest part of what's running in an AI application. This lesson covers everything else it depends on, and what can go wrong before you touch any of it.

A typical AI feature depends on a pretrained model from a public hub, maybe a third-party fine-tuning dataset, open-source orchestration packages, and sometimes plugins from outside your organization. Every one of those is a link in the supply chain — a weakness in any of them becomes a weakness in your application.

A model is just a large file of numbers — someone can fine-tune in a hidden trigger behavior and upload it looking like a normal release. A handful of poisoned examples in a third-party dataset can implant unwanted behavior without being obvious. Package registries have the same typosquatting problems as any ecosystem. Many model hub listings offer no cryptographic proof the weights match what's claimed.

None of this looks like a security decision from the builder's seat. Downloading a model or running a package install feels like routine development, not like accepting an unreviewed third-party binary into production. That mismatch is exactly what makes supply chain risk easy to skip past.

Prefer models with verifiable provenance — published hashes or signed weights. Pin dependency versions with a lockfile. Run vulnerability scanning in CI. Vet third-party datasets before fine-tuning on them. Use a private package mirror for production builds where practical.
Next lesson: insecure output handling — what happens after the model responds, and why trusting that output blindly is its own risk category.
